response.answer: Ensemble conformalized quantile regression (EnCQR) effectively restores PI coverage while preserving trustworthy SHAP attributions. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression (HGPR) also handles heteroscedasticity well. Quantile regression combined with conformal prediction is a strong method for this task.

results.content: EnCQR constructs distribution-free and approximately marginally valid prediction intervals (PIs), which are suitable for nonstationary and heteroscedastic time series data. The results demonstrate that EnCQR outperforms models based only on quantile regression or conformal prediction, and it provides sharper, more informative, and valid PIs. Index Terms—Probabilistic forecasting; time series analysis; uncertainty quantiﬁcation; conformal prediction; quantile regres-sion; heteroscedasticity; ensemble learning; deep neural networks. We directly tackle the challenge of construct-ing adaptive and valid PIs for time series data by combining and leveraging the strengths of quantile regression (QR) and conformal prediction (CP). We refer to a neural network (NN) that performs QR and is optimized with Eq. Conformalized quantile regression (CQR) CQR is a probabilistic forecasting method that combines CP and QR to construct valid PIs for heteroscedastic data [15], [27]. THE ENCQR ALGORITHM The proposed ensemble conformalized quantile regression (EnCQR) algorithm, summarized in Alg. 2, combines an ensemble of QR learners with CP to construct PIs for time series. Similarly to EnbPI, EnCQR utilizes an out-of-sample en-semble prediction strategy to apply CP to time series data, but replaces the aggregated point prediction of EnbPI with aggregated quantile predictions for the upper and lower bound of a PI. 8 1) PI Coverage and PI Width: Both EnCQR and EnbPI successfully construct approximately valid PIs for all time series, demonstrating that they work well for different data distributions, regardless of the regression algorithm used in the ensemble. However, the width of the PIs constructed by EnbPI considerably varies compared to EnCQR, which produces the sharpest valid PIs. This can be explained by referring to the variability measures presented in Table I; For time series with a low degree of heteroscedasticity, the quality of the PIs constructed by EnCQR and EnbPI is approximately equal, whereas for the more heteroscedastic time series, EnCQR constructs signiﬁcantly sharper and more informative PIs. This is illustrated in Fig. 2, which plots PICP against PINAW for the NN- and RF-based models on the Solar and Portugal datasets. In this paper we proposed EnCQR, a probabilistic time series forecasting method that leverages CP to generate PIs with valid coverage and ensemble learners performing QR to handle heteroscedastic data.

While Big Data is bringing new opportunities for regression applications, ignoring this limitation may lead to biased estimators and inaccurate confidence and prediction intervals. This paper aims to study the treatment of non-constant variance in regression models, also known as heteroscedasticity. results.title: Estimation of heteroscedastic measurement noise variances - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Estimation of heteroscedastic measurement noise variances. We propose a procedure to estimate the noise variances starting from the residuals. The outcome of our procedure is an estimate of the noise variances which depends on the sample number, but is independent of the postulated model. This article presents a general procedure to extract heteroscedastic noise information from observations when neither replicates nor a well known variance function are available. Therefore, a correction is included in the procedure to suppress possible model errors and hence make the noise variance estimation relatively independent of the specific model used. This is important because the estimated noise variances may be used in a later step e.g. to detect model errors or in a model selection procedure [8]. In the case of the oceanographic data, estimates of the measurement uncertainties were needed to construct a Weighted Least Squares cost function (more details about the measurements and model are given in Section 3.3). In the next section, the methodology for estimating the heteroscedastic noise variances is presented. After the presentation of the method, its efficiency is assessed on two simulation examples (3.1 Heterogeneous distribution of degrees of freedom, 3.2 Performance of model error correction) and on one real data problem, introducing the oceanographical example (Section 3.3). The method to estimate heteroscedastic noise variances in the presence of (reasonable) model errors was presented, validated on two simulations and applied to a real dataset. The results show that the variance estimations are accurate even when model errors are present, but can still depend on the subset choice and the number of data available. ### Estimation of heteroscedastic variances in linear models. The two methods normally used to estimate variance functions from data — replicate analysis and residuals analysis (via generalized least squares, GLS) — are compared quantitatively through Monte Carlo simulations on simple models having a linear response function (RF) and two different two-parameter variance functions (VFs) — the power model and a components of variance model. The proposed approach not only gives accurate estimates of both the model and error covariance matrix, but also provides answers to the two important issues of data scaling and model order determination.

results.title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression for material structure–property relationship modeling - ScienceDirect
results.content: Uncertainty quantification is a critical aspect of machine learning models for material property predictions. Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) is a popular technique for capturing uncertainties, but most existing models assume homoscedastic aleatoric uncertainty (noise), which may not adequately represent the heteroscedastic behavior observed in real-world datasets. Existing Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression (HGPR) models often employ complicated structures to capture input-dependent noise but may lack interpretability. In this paper, we propose an HGPR approach that combines GPR with polynomial regression-based noise modeling to capture and quantify uncertainties in material property predictions while providing interpretable noise models. By capturing heteroscedastic behavior, enhancing interpretability, and improving model selection, our approach contributes to the development of more robust and reliable machine learning models for material property predictions, enabling informed decision-making in material design and optimization. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) plays a crucial role in assessing the reliability and robustness of machine learning models, particularly in the context of material property predictions to improve the reliability of materials predictions and decisions [1]. The existing literature on Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression (HGPR) models often employs sophisticated model structures to capture input-dependent noise. While Gaussian Process (GP) models have been shown to offer good interpretability in literature, including analytical variance-based global sensitivity analysis in GPs [42], [43], [44], there remains a need for methods that can explicitly model and interpret heteroscedastic noise in materials design contexts. Overly complex heteroscedastic models - those with elaborate structures such as nested Gaussian Processes or integrate different machine learning techniques (like SVR or ELM) - often lack interpretability and computational simplicity in exchange of potentially increased predictive power. Our approach aims to capture and quantify uncertainties in material property predictions while providing a clear functional relationship between the input features and the noise variance. In this study, we propose a heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression (HGPR) model for capturing input-dependent noise patterns in materials modeling. The approach extends the standard Gaussian Process Regression framework by incorporating a polynomial regression method to model the heteroscedastic noise, enhancing uncertainty quantification while preserving the simplicity and interpretability of the model. In this study, we developed a heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression (HGPR) model to capture complex, input-dependent noise patterns in material behavior modeling.
